title: High-Level Thinking
explain: Before drawing any boxes, I characterise the problem with four questions: what goes in and what comes out, whether it is read- or write-heavy, whether it is latency- or throughput-bound, and how fresh reads must be. The answers decide most of the architecture, so I say them out loud and let the design follow.
model:
Four questions, asked in this order, each steering a different part of the design:

| Question | What it steers |
| --- | --- |
| **Input → output**: what comes in, what goes out, what transforms it? | The API and the data flow |
| **Read-heavy or write-heavy?** (rough ratio) | Caches, replicas, precompute vs partitioning, batching, queues |
| **Latency or throughput?** | Per-request paths vs batch pipelines; batching trades one for the other |
| **How strong must consistency be?** | Single leader and transactions vs replicas and async paths |

Then move down to mechanisms with the [low-level decision order](#/sd/f/low-level-decision-order), and spend the most care on the [one-way doors](#/sd/f/one-way-door): API, data flow, data model.

details.q: Why not start with the components you know you will need?
details.a: Because the components are answers to these questions. Drawing Kafka, Redis and Cassandra first commits you to costs (operations, consistency trade-offs) the problem may not need; one Postgres often suffices once you see the load.

details.q: How do you get the read/write ratio when the interviewer has not given one?
details.a: Derive it from user behaviour: actions per user per day for reads and for writes, times daily users, over 86,400 s. State the assumption and the order of magnitude; 10:1 vs 1000:1 matters, 10:1 vs 12:1 does not.

details.q: What does read-heavy push you towards, concretely?
details.a: Doing work at write time so reads are cheap: caching, read replicas, denormalised or precomputed views, CDN. Write-heavy pushes the other way: partitioning writes, batching, append-only logs, queues to absorb bursts.

details.q: Why are latency and throughput in tension?
details.a: The tools that raise throughput — batching, queuing, larger units of work — make each item wait longer. A user-facing request wants small, direct paths; a nightly job wants big batches. Say which one the system optimises before choosing.

details.q: How do you phrase the consistency question so it is useful?
details.a: Per data type and per reader: can *this* reader see *this* data a few seconds stale? Balances and inventory usually no; feeds, counters and search results usually yes. Mixed answers are normal and lead to a mixed design.

details.q: When do these questions stop being enough?
details.a: Once the shape is clear. They set direction; the details (sharding keys, failure handling) come from deep dives on the parts the answers flagged as hard.

prompts.q: An interviewer says: "Design a leaderboard for a mobile game." Run the four questions out loud before proposing anything.
points: Input/output: score submissions in, top-N and a player's rank out
Read/write ratio estimated from players and score updates
Latency target for showing the leaderboard vs submitting a score
Consistency: can ranks lag a few seconds? (usually yes)
Says how each answer will shape the design

prompts.q: Explain why you ask these questions before choosing components, as you would to an interviewer who wants you to get going.
points: Components are answers to these questions
Avoids paying for complexity the load does not need
Takes a minute and sets the direction for the whole interview
Shows the interviewer how you reason, not just what you know

prompts.q: Take one system you know (e.g. a URL shortener or a chat app) and say what each of the four answers implies for its design.
points: Names the input, the output and the core transformation
Gives a read/write ratio and its consequence
Picks latency or throughput and says why
States the consistency need per data type
